title: Reusability report: multi-sample omics network inference operates in distinct robustness regimes defined by prior knowledge and data availability - Nature Machine Intelligence
text:
Download PDF

AbstractKnowledge-constrained network inference enables the reconstruction of regulatory programmes from high-dimensional biological data, yet the conditions under which shared and context-specific structures can be reliably identified remain poorly understood. Pablo Rodriguez-Mier et al. recently introduced CORNETO, a framework for multi-sample constrained inference. Here we reproduce, evaluate and extend CORNETO in terms of robustness, identifiability and bias–variance trade-offs. Using dynamic haematopoiesis and stable cortical datasets, we systematically assess four network reconstruction paradigms while preserving the original method-specific evaluation procedures and benchmark definitions. We show that multi-sample inference generally improves robustness and reproducibility, although gains in predictive performance depend on biological context and the completeness of the prior network. To enhance stability, we introduce bootstrap aggregation and selective re-expansion strategies that improve consensus robustness and recovery while preserving context-specific signals without modifying the underlying optimization scheme or sacrificing generality. Across datasets and methods, our results reveal distinct inference regimes governed by sample availability, prior knowledge and regularization. Together, these findings position network reconstruction as a regime-dependent learning problem and provide practical principles for robust multi-sample biological network inference.

MainInferring regulatory networks from high-dimensional biological data is fundamentally underdetermined, as several candidate regulatory structures may be consistent with the same observed measurements. As a result, predictive performance alone cannot establish that an inferred network corresponds to the underlying molecular regulatory mechanism. In practice, understanding biological systems requires methods that capture context-dependent interactions among genes, proteins and metabolites1, in which nodes are molecular entities and edges represent functional interactions2. Because interactions vary across cell types and conditions, accurate network inference is essential for understanding cellular processes, diseases and treatment responses3,4. Yet, several network configurations can explain the same observations, making it ill-posed to distinguish shared and context-specific structure.To meet the associated challenges, methods for inferring networks fall into two categories: data-driven and knowledge-driven. Data-driven models offer strong predictive power but typically require large datasets and are often difficult to interpret5,6,7,8,9,10. Knowledge-driven methods leverage prior-knowledge networks (PKNs), which improves interpretability and enables inference in sparse-data settings, but they are often tailored to specific network types and applied per sample11,12,13. Notably, per-sample inference may complicate the identification of robust shared versus context-specific structure, as several network solutions can explain the same observations under noisy or weakly constrained settings. Although shared patterns can be identified by overlapping independently inferred sample-specific networks, such approaches may remain sensitive to instability and variability. Although the original CORNETO study extensively analysed the advantages and trade-offs of multi-sample coupling, the robustness, extensibility and optimization behaviour of these approaches across distinct biological regimes remain incompletely characterized.Constrained optimization for the recovery of networks from omics (CORNETO)14 provides a unified, knowledge-driven framework that reformulates multi-sample network inference as a mixed-integer constrained optimization problem based on network flows. This enables joint inference of shared and condition-specific subnetworks via structured sparsity penalties, thereby stabilizing reconstruction and reducing solution variability and yielding sparser, more interpretable models. Moreover, CORNETO unifies several methods—flux balance analysis (FBA)15, sparse FBA (sFBA)16,17, integrative metabolic analysis tool (iMAT)18, causal reasoning for network identification using integer value programming (CARNIVAL)19 and prize-collecting Steiner trees (PCSTs)20—as special cases of a single formulation, and it provides an open-source implementation that supports modular extensions.Here we build upon the work of Pablo Rodriguez-Mier et al. by systematically evaluating the computational reusability, robustness, reproducibility and practical behaviour of the CORNETO framework (Fig. 1a,b). Our primary objective is not to systematically validate the biological correctness of the inferred regulatory mechanisms, for which comprehensive experimental ground truths are unavailable, but to characterize when and why multi-sample constrained inference produces stable and reproducible solutions across different inference and data settings. We then extend this evaluation by systematically applying the compatible CORNETO formulations to complementary biological settings: a dynamic haematopoietic differentiation dataset21 and a comparatively stable adult brain cortex dataset22. These systems represent contrasting regimes of transcriptional variability and intersample heterogeneity, allowing us to investigate how biological context influences the behaviour of constrained multi-sample inference; in this selection, the latter case is a stringent test due to the limited gene-expression variability23,24.Fig. 1: Overview of CORNETO framework reproducibility, reusability, constraints and refinement strategies.Full size imagea, Reproducibility of the CORNETO workflow across multi-omics datasets (proteomics, phosphoproteomics and scRNA-seq) and model organisms, showing integration of metabolic (sFBA and iMAT), signalling (CARNIVAL and Steiner tree/prize-collecting Steiner forest (PCSF)) and PPI-based (KPNN) inference tools. b, Reusability of CORNETO in human single-cell datasets spanning dynamic (haematopoiesis) and stable (brain) systems, illustrating four applications: metabolic inference, PPI module discovery, signalling optimization and causal signalling reconstruction. c, Robustness bottlenecks across inference regimes. CORNETO performance is influenced by sparse or imbalanced data, incomplete PKNs, and the number of jointly modelled conditions. These factors affect identifiability, the recoverable signal, PPV and TPR, and the Jaccard stability, defining the regime in which constrained network inference operates. d, Matched refinement strategies for robust CORNETO inference. The regime diagnosis from c guides pre- and post-inference actions, including bootstrap aggregation to reduce stochastic variability and improve consensus robustness, selective re-expansion to recover informative features lost after aggressive pruning, and prior- and condition-aware tuning to balance regularization and improve stable active-network recovery. Together, these strategies improve robustness, sparsity and network interpretability without changing the core CORNETO framework.Source dataFor each case study, we systematically evaluated the computational robustness, stability and sensitivity of CORNETO formulations using iMAT, CARNIVAL, Steiner tree and knowledge-primed neural networks (KPNNs)25. Biological relevance was assessed separately and only when established biological relations provided an interpretable reference. Each tool addresses distinct biological questions: metabolic flux consistency, signalling propagation, protein interaction modules and neural-network-based regulatory inference (Fig. 1b). Importantly, these frameworks do not produce directly equivalent outputs and were, therefore, not compared using a single unified ground-truth objective. Instead, each method was evaluated within shared biological contexts using framework-appropriate inputs, optimization objectives and evaluation criteria. Our goal was not to rank methods against a common target but to characterize their robustness, behaviour and sensitivity under controlled multi-sample settings. Inputs, outputs, optimization objectives, prior-network definitions and evaluation metrics for each framework are summarized in Supplementary Table 1. Additionally, to assess performance across different levels of data coverage and network complexity, we tested framework robustness under challenging input conditions (Fig. 1c), including imbalanced subpopulations26,27, smaller datasets28 and variations in PKNs29,30,31.Finally, we investigated practical strategies for improving the robustness and interpretability of CORNETO-derived solutions (Fig. 1d). Beyond evaluating the effects of prior-network completeness and sample availability, we introduced a bootstrap aggregation procedure32 to stabilize stochastic optimization and selective re-expansion to recover informative features lost during aggressive pruning. These adaptations improved recall, interpretability33 and predictive accuracy while preserving sparsity, demonstrating the flexibility of CORNETO in incorporating modular improvements.Together, these analyses characterize constrained multi-sample network reconstruction as a regime-dependent learning problem, demonstrating that the benefits of joint inference depend on the interplay among prior knowledge, biological heterogeneity, regularization and data availability, and they provide practical guidance for applying and extending CORNETO across diverse biological contexts.ResultsEvaluating the reproducibility of the reported resultsWe reproduced the original CORNETO results (Methods, Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 2), confirming that CORNETO accurately reconstructs context-specific subnetworks within prior-constrained optimization spaces derived from multi-sample omics data. As CORNETO is not a single method but rather a framework integrating several optimization- and network-based approaches, we refer readers to Methods and Supplementary Table 1 and to the original article for a detailed description of each component method and, equally important, the associated evaluations used during the initial reproduction analyses. Quantitative evaluations followed the same benchmarking procedures, validation criteria and reference definitions implemented in the original method-specific codebases and benchmark scripts. In all analyses, the PKN defined the constrained, feasible optimization space, consistent with the original implementations, but was not treated as a universal biological ground truth. In the following sections, we explicitly indicate any modifications introduced relative to the original implementation, including changes to input data, prior networks, optimization settings or evaluation metrics; those modifications are also summarized in Supplementary Table 1.Regarding reproducibility, certain CORNETO tools, including FBA and KPNN34, are inherently stochastic due to optimization heuristics or neural network training35. To assess the impact of this stochasticity on inference stability, we repeated both single- and multi-sample analyses several times using the original datasets and compared outcomes across independent runs.For FBA, multi-sample sFBA consistently generated smaller networks than single-condition FBA, indicating more compact and robust network inference (Supplementary Fig. 2a). Network reduction depended on the minimum biomass constraint: lower biomass thresholds allow greater flexibility to remove non-essential reactions, whereas near-optimal growth requires other reactions to sustain a high flux. At 10% of the optimal biomass, the networks were reduced by ~32%, whereas at 90%, the reduction decreased to ~6% (Supplementary Fig. 2b). This was accompanied by increased variability across runs, with the coefficient of variation rising from 2.9% to 8.9% (Supplementary Fig. 2c), reflecting greater solution degeneracy near-optimal growth, as several alternative flux distributions can satisfy the constraint.For KPNN, using the T-cell-receptor stimulation dataset, the scores for the area under the curve of the receiver operating characteristic (ROC-AUC)36 remained highly stable across repeated runs, both before and after pruning, indicating the minimal impact of training stochasticity on predictive performance (Supplementary Fig. 2d). The per-run performance deviation (ΔROC-AUC < 0.001) was negligible (Supplementary Fig. 2e), further demonstrating the reproducibility of network inference using KPNN under fixed data splits.In summary, although some CORNETO components involve stochastic optimization or neural network training and are, therefore, sensitive to the initialization seeds, the multi-sample formulation consistently reduced run-to-run variability and produced more stable and reproducible network reconstructions than the corresponding single-sample implementations. These results support the use of multi-sample constrained inference as a robustness-enhancing strategy for integrative, multi-condition omics studies.Assessing CORNETO across dynamic and stable biological systemsWe next evaluated CORNETO as an integrated framework by applying all feasible tools to two biologically complementary contexts: a dynamic system (haematopoiesis) and a steady-state scenario (brain tissue).The first context represents a biological regime characterized by continuous state transitions. We analysed four single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) samples derived from human CD34+ haematopoietic progenitor cells, annotated into erythroid, monocytic, lymphoid and megakaryocytic differentiation states (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 3a). We defined cell-type-specific contrasts by treating each cell type as the target condition relative to the others. This shared contrast design was applied uniformly to iMAT, KPNN, Steiner tree and CARNIVAL to evaluate whether the multi-sample approach of CORNETO improves interpretability and robustness in a dynamic developmental context (see Supplementary Table 1 for the overall details).Fig. 2: Evaluation of CORNETO tools in the haematopoiesis differentiation system.Full size imagea, Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) of haematopoietic populations across four donors for HSC, CLP, PreB, GMP, MDP, ERP and MEP. b, iMAT precision and recall for several λ values. c, KPNN classification accuracy, precision and recall before and after pruning, alongside changes in network size. d, Steiner tree reconstructions using 5, 20 or 50 terminal genes, showing fitting error versus recovery of prior-knowledge edges for single- and multi-sample settings. e, CARNIVAL reconstructions across all pairwise contrasts, showing fitting error versus recovered edges for several regularization strengths.Source dataFor iMAT, which infers active metabolic states from gene-expression-derived constraints, we evaluated the regularization weight λ, a key parameter governing the multi-sample formulation and its added value relative to independent sample optimization. Specifically, λ controls the extent to which flux distributions are encouraged to be similar across samples (for a low λ, each sample is fitted independently, whereas for a high λ, flux profiles are forced to converge) (Fig. 2b), using the same benchmark definitions and evaluation procedures implemented in the original reference framework (‘Evaluation metrics and reference definitions’ in Methods). Across λ values, the positive predictive value (PPV) and true positive rate (TPR) remained low with limited variation (maximum PPV ≈ 0.20 and maximum TPR ≈ 0.042). Modest regularization (λ ≈ 0.1–0.25) yielded the best performance, with a slight increase in PPV (~0.17–0.18) and stable TPR (~0.034–0.038). Stronger regularization (λ ≥ 0.75) markedly reduced both metrics, indicating over-regularization. The apparent PPV increase at λ = 1.5 reflects excessive sparsity rather than improved recovery. These trends and further analyses (Supplementary Fig. 3d,e) support the use of moderate λ values to balance robustness and biological variability.Conversely, the KPNN, which uses the PKN as a scaffold to construct a cell-type predictive model, achieved strong supervised performance for cell-type classification (accuracy, macro F1, precision and recall all >0.9; Fig. 2c) using curated cell-type annotations provided with the dataset as the supervised target. Because KPNN learns a shared representation across all cells, it provides an opportunity to assess whether network-constrained compression can retain predictive information derived from several samples while improving model interpretability. Although predictive accuracy and network sparsity do not fully capture the biological objectives of KPNN models, we analysed these quantities as practical indicators of optimization behaviour, representation efficiency and the trade-offs introduced by biologically constrained pruning. After CORNETO-based structural pruning, supervised classification performance decreased substantially (accuracy ≈ 0.58, macro F1 ≈ 0.42, precision ≈ 0.49 and recall ≈ 0.42), reflecting the impact of aggressive sparsification. This pruning substantially reduced network complexity, from 9,791 inputs and ~83,000 edges to 66 inputs and 267 edges (Supplementary Table 2). Importantly, pruning also altered feature prioritization: differentiation-associated genes lost prominence, whereas more general metabolic or structural genes gained prominence (Supplementary Fig. 3f,g). These findings suggest that although multi-sample learning captures robust shared signals, aggressive pruning improves interpretability at the expense of cell-type-specific regulatory programmes.For the Steiner tree task, which identifies a minimum-cost regulatory subnetwork connecting predefined terminal genes via informative intermediate nodes and edges, we evaluated the multi-sample formulation of CORNETO by varying the number of terminals (5, 20 and 50) and comparing multi- versus single-sample inference. Across all settings, multi-sample inference consistently achieved a lower fitting error for the same fraction of active edges within the constrained prior network (Fig. 2d, combined view). This advantage increased with network complexity (20–50 terminals), as multi-sample reconstructions recovered a larger fraction of reference-consistent edges within the constrained prior network (~0.3–0.6) at comparable or lower error (~0.05–0.15). By contrast, single-sample performance degraded sharply as the number of terminals increased (Supplementary Fig. 3b), reflecting sensitivity to noise. Moreover, multi-sample optimization showed smoother convergence and reduced variability (Supplementary Fig. 3c). Joint inference across haematopoiesis replicates yielded up to ×2–3 higher edge recovery without increased error, indicating that shared structural constraints stabilize reconstruction under matched conditions.We next applied CARNIVAL to infer upstream signalling pathways from differential expression across haematopoietic lineages using the all-versus-all contrast design. To assess the added value of jointly modelling several samples, we compared single-sample and multi-sample formulations across a range of regularization strengths. Multi-sample CARNIVAL consistently achieved a lower fitting error for the same proportion of recovered active edges within the constrained signalling prior (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. 4a). This advantage was most apparent at moderate regularization (λ ≈ 0.05–0.2), as multi-sample solutions recovered substantially more reference-consistent edges within the constrained signalling prior at comparable error. For instance, at λ = 0.1, the multi-sample model retained ~720 shared edges, compared with ~470–500 in single-sample runs, with similar fitting errors (Supplementary Fig. 4a). As λ increased, both formulations exhibited the expected sparsity versus accuracy trade-off, but the multi-sample performance curve declined more gradually and remained more stable across regularization strengths, indicating that information sharing across samples improves robustness and preserves signalling structure under stronger regularization.We then evaluated a second case study based on adult brain cortex single-cell data (Supplementary Note 1), representing a comparatively stable biological system with limited transcriptional variability. In this setting, the biological impact of multi-sample regularization was less pronounced. (1) For iMAT, both PPV and TPR remained low across λ values (maximum PPV ≈ 0.12 and maximum TPR ≈ 0.027), with modest gains at intermediate regularization (λ ≈ 0.1–0.25), reflecting the constrained metabolic dynamic range of steady-state neuronal populations. (2) KPNN achieved strong baseline classification performance (macro F1 ≈ 0.94), but CORNETO-based pruning reduced class-balanced metrics (macro F1 ≈ 0.80) and shifted feature importance from neuron-specific regulators of neurogenesis and synaptic function (for example, FOXG1, TBR1 and SATB2) towards more general transcriptional control genes. (3) Multi-sample Steiner tree inference yielded more stable subnetworks than independently inferred single-sample runs, yielding more coherent subnetworks that emphasized common neuronal regulatory backbones, although without the clear biologically ordered gradients observed in haematopoiesis. (4) CARNIVAL did not return feasible solutions, probably due to extreme intercell-type homogeneity and class imbalance, which generated a highly degenerate optimization space incompatible with its bounded formulation.Together, these findings suggest that the biological value of the multi-sample framework in CORNETO depends on the structure of the variability present in the data. In haematopoiesis, where differentiation generates coordinated but distinct regulatory states, joint inference reveals developmental relations that are consistently recovered across complementary methods. By contrast, adult brain populations share more conserved transcriptional programmes, limiting the extent to which further biological structure can be extracted through sample coupling. These two case studies illustrate contrasting behaviours of constrained multi-sample inference. For the haematopoietic dataset, characterized by coordinated differentiation-associated variation, sample coupling provided clearer gains in network stability and biological interpretability, whereas for the adult cortical dataset, these gains were more limited. Because each setting is represented by a single dataset, these observations should not be interpreted as establishing general differences between dynamic and homeostatic biological systems. Rather, they motivate the hypothesis that the value of multi-sample coupling depends on the structure and magnitude of biological variability present in the data.However, because comprehensive ground-truth regulatory interactions are unavailable for these developmental systems, these observations should be interpreted as supportive and hypothesis-generating rather than as definitive evidence of a causal regulatory structure.Assessing the biological value of multi-sample network inference across diverse cellular contextsTo determine whether the inferred networks captured biologically meaningful organization rather than merely improving the optimization metrics, we examined how the resulting subnetworks reflect known relations among haematopoietic cell states.For CARNIVAL, we focused on erythroid differentiation from the haematopoiesis dataset by comparing subnetworks inferred for megakaryocyte–erythroid progenitor (MEP) versus erythroid progenitor (ERP), multipotent progenitor (MPP), haematopoietic stem cell (HSC) and all contrasts. Subnetworks were encoded as edge-incidence vectors and projected into the principal component analysis space, with pairwise similarity matrices computed across regularization strengths (Supplementary Fig. 4b,c). Multi-sample CARNIVAL recovered signalling programmes that largely followed the expected developmental hierarchy. MEP–ERP, representing adjacent differentiation states, produced the most coherent and tightly clustered subnetworks, whereas MEP–MPP and MEP–HSC contrasts showed progressively greater divergence. The broad MEP–all comparison exhibited the weakest structural coherence, reflecting the aggregation of several haematopoietic lineages (Supplementary Note 2). These observations suggest that CARNIVAL captures regulatory relations that mirror developmental proximity and may, therefore, be useful for identifying signalling programmes associated with lineage commitment.We next examined the multi-sample Steiner tree formulation using the same contrasts (Supplementary Fig. 5a–d). Like CARNIVAL, the MEP–ERP comparison yielded the most compact and coherent subnetworks, characterized by high connectivity among erythroid-associated regulators and low fitting errors. By contrast, MEP–MPP and MEP–HSC comparisons produced progressively larger and more diffuse subnetworks, consistent with increasing regulatory divergence from earlier progenitor states, whereas MEP–all generated the least specific structure (Supplementary Note 3). Unlike CARNIVAL, which emphasizes causal signalling consistency, Steiner tree highlighted the minimal network backbone required to connect differentiation-associated factors, providing a complementary view of the regulatory architecture underlying lineage transitions.Taken together, the two approaches converged on the same biological interpretation despite relying on distinct optimization principles. Both recovered network structures are consistent with the known haematopoietic differentiation hierarchy, suggesting that multi-sample inference enhances the identification of robust lineage-associated regulatory programmes. CARNIVAL primarily resolved signalling relations and their consistency across contrasts, whereas Steiner tree emphasized the connectivity structure linking differentiation-associated regulators.Strategies for improving robustness and interpretabilityOur analyses identified two recurring challenges in constrained network inference: stochastic variability arising from optimization and information loss due to overly aggressive sparsification. Although these effects did not prevent CORNETO from recovering biologically meaningful structure, they can reduce reproducibility and obscure moderately informative features. We, therefore, investigated whether robustness and interpretability could be augmented through post-inference refinement strategies that operate on the inferred solutions rather than modifying the underlying optimization framework. To this end, we evaluated two complementary approaches: bootstrap aggregation to improve stability and selective re-expansion to recover informative biological structure.Bootstrap aggregation improves stability and recallWe first investigated whether bootstrapped-based aggregation could reduce stochastic variability and improve the robustness of inferred networks. Using the sFBA framework with the MitoCore metabolic model and single-reaction knockout simulations, we repeatedly resampled intervention conditions and performed inference under both single-sample and multi-sample configurations. Reaction activation frequencies were then computed across bootstrap replicates, with reactions active in more >80% of runs classified as robust, and reactions recovered only through aggregation classified as expansion edges (Fig. 3a). Across all ensembles, both configurations achieved higher recall and network completeness than single-run baselines: in an eight-condition setting, bootstrapping recovered another 8–11 reactions per model (~8–11% expansion) while preserving more than 85% overlap with high-confidence baseline edges (Fig. 3b, top). These expansions complemented rather than replaced the original solutions, and reaction-level frequencies showed reduced stochastic variability, with ensemble-averaged solutions converging towards a stable subset of shared reactions. Importantly, increasing the number of resampled conditions to 16 led to saturation, with little extra recovery of robust edges (Fig. 3b, bottom). At this point, single- and multi-sample configurations approached a fully constrained solution space, with the global overlap stabilizing at ~82% and ~89%, respectively. These findings indicate that bootstrap aggregation suppresses stochastic variability and consolidates reproducible network structure, with the strongest benefits observed in the multi-sample setting (Supplementary Fig. 6a,b).Fig. 3: Pre- and post-inference refinement can improve robustness.Full size imagea, Reaction-level robustness across single-sample and multi-sample sFBA. Higher similarity indicates reduced sensitivity to the specific subset of conditions selected. rep, repetition.Source dataSelective re-expansion recovers informative biological structureWe next examined a complementary challenge arising from aggressive sparsification. Although pruning substantially improves model compactness and interpretability, it can also remove moderately informative biological features that contribute to predictive performance. To determine whether such information could be recovered without abandoning sparsity, we evaluated a selective re-expansion strategy using the KPNN framework applied to the haematopoietic scRNA-seq dataset. Specifically, we reintroduced the top 100 most informative genes, ranked according to expression-based importance, that had been excluded from the pruned CORNETO directed acyclic graph. This targeted re-expansion increased the active edge set from 267 to 11,924, yet it remained substantially smaller than the original network. Importantly, predictive performance improved markedly: classification accuracy increased from 0.576 to 0.906, macro F1 increased from 0.424 to 0.848, and both precision and recall exceeded 0.84 (Supplementary Table 2). These results suggest that the performance losses observed after pruning are not solely attributable to the reduced model size but also to the removal of moderately informative genes that collectively contribute to lineage discrimination. Selective re-expansion therefore provides a practical mechanism for restoring biologically relevant information while preserving much of the interpretability gained through network compression.Better defined prior-network improves robustnessBeyond post-inference refinement, increasing prior-network completeness also improves constrained inference. Rather than artificially augmenting existing PKNs, we progressively removed edges from the Human-GEM reaction graph before multi-condition iMAT optimization, thereby simulating different levels of prior-network incompleteness. Decreasing the graph completeness removed held-out positive reaction-activity labels from the optimization graph, thereby reducing the recoverable evaluation signal (Fig. 3c). This loss of prior structure directly impaired precision–recall performance: at 20% graph completeness, all runs returned zero active reactions and produced no valid precision–recall points; at 40–60% completeness, the model recovered only a limited signal across λ values; whereas 80–100% completeness enabled higher precision and recall across a broader range of regularization strengths (Fig. 3d). These results show that prior-network completeness strongly determines the quality of the constrained metabolic inference and that regularization becomes useful only when sufficient prior structure remains available.Increasing the number of jointly modelled conditions improves robustnessWe next tested whether increasing the number of jointly optimized conditions stabilizes inference under repeated condition subsampling (Fig. 3e). Using iMAT, we randomly selected groups of 2, 4, 8 or 16 haematopoietic pseudobulk conditions and quantified active-reaction set stability using pairwise Jaccard similarity between active-reaction sets inferred from independent subsampling runs. Increasing the number of jointly inferred conditions generally increased the similarity between independently inferred solutions and reduced the sensitivity to the specific subset of conditions selected. Complementary analyses showed that increasing the number of conditions also stabilized the inferred network size and reduced the sensitivity to λ across repeated runs (Supplementary Note 4). Together, these results show that prior-network completeness and sample and/or condition availability jointly shape the robustness and reproducibility of constrained multi-condition network inference.Together, these analyses demonstrate that pre- and post-inference refinement can substantially improve both robustness and biological interpretability without altering the underlying CORNETO optimization framework. Although demonstrated here in a subset of tools, all strategies reflect general principles that are broadly applicable across CORNETO inference tasks and data modalities. These results suggest that robustness can be improved not only through optimization design but also through a principled refinement of inferred solutions, providing a practical path towards more stable and biologically informative network reconstructions.DiscussionIn this study, we reproduced and extended the original CORNETO framework, and we confirmed the reproducibility of its optimization pipelines across several inference paradigms. Consistent with the original work, all analyses followed the published benchmarking procedures, validation criteria and evaluation metrics. Our primary objective was not to establish new biological ground truths but to evaluate how multi-sample constrained inference affects robustness and stability across diverse data regimes.Across iMAT, KPNN, Steiner tree and CARNIVAL, the principal benefit of multi-sample inference was improved robustness rather than uniformly improved predictive performance. Joint optimization reduced the sensitivity to stochastic variability and regularization by producing more stable and reproducible solutions when samples had a partially overlapping regulatory structure. However, these advantages depend strongly on data characteristics, including prior-network completeness and intersample heterogeneity, indicating that multi-sample coupling is most effective when sufficient shared structure exists across samples.The haematopoietic and brain case studies illustrate these operating regimes. Multi-sample inference provided clear advantages for the dynamic haematopoietic system, whereas gains were more limited for the comparatively stable adult brain. These analyses were intended primarily to evaluate inference behaviour under distinct biological settings rather than to establish new regulatory mechanisms. More broadly, the lack of experimentally validated context-specific regulatory ground truths remains a principal limitation for network-inference benchmarking. Consequently, our conclusions focus on the robustness, reproducibility and identifiability of inferred solutions rather than realizing a definitive recovery of the causal regulatory interactions.An important limitation of this study is its biological breadth. The contrasting dynamic and comparatively stable settings are represented by individual haematopoietic and cortical datasets and, therefore, constitute case studies rather than biological replicates of these broader system classes. Consequently, our observations regarding the influence of biological variability should be regarded as hypotheses about inference regimes rather than general properties of dynamic and homeostatic tissues. Establishing such generality will require systematic evaluation across several independent datasets, tissues, organisms and PKNs. Similarly, the biological analyses performed here assess consistency with established biological relations but do not constitute an experimental validation of the inferred causal regulatory mechanisms.We show that robustness can be enhanced through both pre- and result-level refinement strategies. Bootstrap aggregation reduced stochastic variability and increased the recovery of reproducible network components, whereas selective re-expansion mitigated information loss from aggressive pruning. Additionally, a better prior network enhanced robustness. Together with the operating-regime framework summarized in Fig. 4, these results provide practical guidance for selecting regularization strategies and interpreting CORNETO outputs across different biological contexts.Fig. 4: Case-study-informed factors influencing robustness in multi-sample constrained network inference.Full size imageDecision matrix summarizing recommended inference tools, regularization strategies and refinements based on system dynamics, data density and sample availability. Dynamic, multi-sample settings favour joint inference, whereas static or sparse regimes require more conservative tool selection and regularization. Bootstrap aggregation and selective re-expansion improve robustness without altering the core optimization framework. The relations summarized here are conceptual principles derived from the computational perturbation analyses and the two biological case studies examined in this work. They are intended as practical hypotheses for CORNETO use rather than as systematically validated distinctions between dynamic and homeostatic biological systems.Source dataThis illustrates how data sparsity, prior completeness and sample availability jointly determine the stability of inference and provides actionable guidance for tuning CORNETO in specific biological contexts. Looking forwards, these principles motivate the development of adaptive regularization, data-driven sparsification and iterative refinement strategies embedded in agentic or human-in-the-loop workflows37, positioning CORNETO as an evolving optimization backbone for scalable, knowledge-driven network inference38,39,40,41,42.Overall, our study highlights robustness as the primary advantage of multi-sample knowledge-constrained inference. By characterizing the conditions under which sample coupling improves stability and introducing practical strategies for enhancing robustness, we provide a framework for applying CORNETO more reliably across diverse biological settings27.MethodsReproducing the original CORNETO frameworkWe reproduced the CORNETO framework using the official implementation available on GitHub (https://github.com/saezlab/corneto) and its companion repository containing all reproducibility scripts and benchmark configurations (https://github.com/saezlab/corneto-manuscript-experiments). All analyses were performed with CORNETO v.1.0.0, Python 3.12.10 and the Gurobi 12.0.2 optimization solver on a Linux high-performance computing environment. Solver precision and configuration parameters were kept identical to those in the reference study (absolute mixed-integer programming (MIP) gap of 1 × 10−6). We adhered strictly to the parameterizations, objective formulations and graph specifications described in the original CORNETO article, fully replicating the canonical implementations for the four methods evaluated in this study: iMAT18, KPNNs25, Steiner tree20 and CARNIVAL19.A comparative summary of the evaluated CORNETO paradigms, including inputs, outputs, optimization objectives, prior-network definitions and evaluation metrics, is provided in Supplementary Table 1.sFBAAll analyses for the sFBA16,17 task were performed using the MitoCore43 v.1.0.1 metabolic model, a manually curated genome-scale reconstruction of human mitochondrial metabolism defining 324 metabolites and 553 reactions encompassing transport, exchange and mitochondrial biochemical processes. The model was obtained in the miom format used by CORNETO from the MIOM-GEMS repository (https://github.com/pablormier/miom-gems), ensuring full compatibility with the CORNETO framework for metabolic network optimization. In addition to the base model, a dataset of single-reaction knockout simulations (mitocore.csv) quantified the effect of each reaction on biomass production, including the reaction identifier, optimal biomass flux after knockout and the number of active reactions in the resulting minimal network. The pruning stage required approximately 243 min and represented the dominant computational bottleneck. KPNN experiments were performed on a workstation equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 8000 GPU (48 GB memory) and dual Intel Xeon Gold 6230R CPUs (52 cores in total). Although neural network training benefited from GPU acceleration, pruning complexity was dominated by discrete mixed-integer optimization.Result-level enhancement due to bootstrapped sFBA expansionTo assess and improve the robustness of flux-based predictions made by CORNETO, we implemented a bootstrapped sFBA framework designed to quantify the stability of inferred reactions and identify reproducible yet subthreshold interactions across repeated resamplings. All analyses were conducted on the haematopoietic metabolic model derived from the MitoCore v.1.0.1 network, which was used as the flux optimization backbone. The experiments were performed on the IBEX High-Performance Computing Cluster using Python 3.11, CORNETO v.1.0 and the Gurobi 12.0.2 solver.Model set-upThe metabolic graph was constructed from the MitoCore v.1.0.1 model containing 647 reactions and 446 metabolites and encoded as a bipartite graph within CORNETO. The biomass export reaction (EX_biomass_e) was used as the objective function, and the associated flux variable served as the quantitative measure of system viability. All flux bounds were initialized using the default lower and upper limits in the model. Optimization was conducted under two configurations: a single-sample sFBA, in which each perturbation was solved independently, and a multi-sample sFBA, where all perturbations were jointly optimized with a shared sparsity constraint to enforce consistency across samples. In both cases, sparsity was introduced through binary indicator variables to enforce near-minimal flux activation per reaction. The solver tolerance was fixed at 10−6, and all optimization problems were solved using mixed-integer programming with integrality focus enabled.Intervention definitionSingle-reaction knockouts were simulated by constraining fluxes to zero for each reaction individually. For each knockout, a baseline optimization was performed to compute the maximum achievable biomass flux followed by a sparse optimization that enforcing a minimum proportion of this flux (90%) to identify the minimal number of active reactions compatible with near-optimal growth. Reactions whose removal reduced the feasible objective by more than 0.1% but did not completely abolish the flux were retained as informative interventions. This filtering produced the subset of approximately 200 perturbations used for the bootstrap analyses, referred to as the intervention set.Bootstrap sampling and executionTo quantify stability, a bootstrap resampling procedure was applied in which subsets of the intervention set were repeatedly sampled with replacement. For each bootstrap replicate, sFBA was executed under both single- and multi-sample configurations using the same solver parameters and sparsity regularization (α = 1.0). A total of 20 bootstrap replicates (B = 20) were performed for each experimental configuration. The number of simultaneous intervention conditions per bootstrap iteration was varied among 2, 4, 8 and 16, enabling an evaluation of how the diversity of perturbations influenced robustness and coverage.For each replicate, binary reaction-activity matrices were generated by thresholding the optimized flux magnitudes at |flux| ≥ 10−6. Reaction-level activation frequencies were computed across bootstrap replicates, producing ‘robustness frequency’ profiles. Reactions active in at least 80% of bootstrap replicates (frequency > 0.8) were classified as robust, whereas those emerging only after aggregation (not active in individual runs but appearing after frequency averaging) were designated as expansion edges.Statistical quantification and robustness metricsTo quantify reproducibility, pairwise overlaps between robust reaction sets across bootstrap replicates were computed using the Jaccard similarity, and the mean overlap within each subset size was used to evaluate within-group consistency. The global overlap, defined as the intersection over the union of all robust reaction sets across all bootstrap runs, measured the degree of convergence between independent ensembles. Across all configurations, the global overlap stabilized at approximately 82% for single-sample sFBA and 89% for multi-sample sFBA, indicating higher reproducibility under the multi-sample coupling scheme.Reaction-level statistics were also aggregated across subset sizes. For each reaction, the median, mean and standard deviation of its activation frequency across bootstrap replicates were computed separately for single- and multi-sample settings. Other stability indices, such as the robust count (number of replicates exceeding the 0.8 threshold) and robust score (product of mean frequency and normalized replicate count), were used to identify highly stable reactions. These metrics were summarized across the ten independent repetitions per subset size and exported as per-reaction and per-size summary tables.Computational scaling and convergenceEach optimization run was executed with a 400-s time limit and default Gurobi heuristics (MIPGap = 0.01). Warm-start options were used when available to accelerate convergence between iterations. The solver runtime, number of binary variables and convergence status were recorded for each configuration and used to characterize the computational scalability.The bootstrap frequency matrices, reaction-level stability summaries and graphical overlays depicting robust reactions across bootstrap replicates were generated using NumPy, pandas and Matplotlib. Statistical analyses were performed using Python-based data pipelines, and all outputs—including bootstrap result tables, robustness profiles and visualization PDFs—were archived for the reproducibility and downstream analysis.Reporting summaryFurther information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Data availability

The haematopoiesis dataset is available via the Gene Expression Omnibus under accession GSE180298 and was originally reported by Ainciburu et al.21. The brain single-cell dataset is available via the CZ CELLxGENE Discover portal (https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/collections/283d65eb-dd53-496d-adb7-7570c7caa443) and corresponds to the dataset reported by Siletti et al.22. All other datasets used for the reproducibility analyses are those described and provided with the original CORNETO framework14. Source data are provided with this paper.
